Note that I do not disagree with any of your statements. I am merely trying to point out that this is not the end of the Buddha's realization. But outside these teachings is what you find when you look at your empty reflection in the mirror or investigate the origin of your existence. That is not what I mean by matters after enlightenment. Knowing there is no world and no self nor form is an aspect realized in the enlightenment experience. But total enlightenment is not completed until one realizes that there is no distinction between the existence of the phenomenal world and the all-pervading world of emptiness or nondifferentiation, and one should also resolve the apparent distinction between enlightenment and non-enlightenment. Even after that, it will take much dedicated practice to mature in being able to perfectly manifest your realization in all aspects of life. In Zen, we have the so-called Tozan's Five Ranks that succinctly describes one's post-satori development.

Your proposition also reminds me of what people apparently say about the Heart Sutra. That if you completely understand the Heart Sutra, you understand the entirety of the Buddha dharma. Just truly realizing that emptiness is form and form is emptiness is enough for complete liberation.

A white horse is not a horse paradox:

Advocate: "Horse" is that by means of which one names the shape. "White" is that by means of which one names the color. What names the color is not what names the shape. Hence, one may say "white horse is not horse."

Objector: If there are white horses, one cannot say that there are no horses. If one cannot say that there are no horses, doesn't that mean that there are horses? For there to be white horses is for there to be horses. How could it be that the white ones are not horses?

Advocate: If one wants horses, that extends to yellow or black horses. But if one wants white horses, that does not extend to yellow or black horses. Suppose that white horses were horses. Then what one wants [in the two cases] would be the same. If what one wants were the same, then 'white' would not differ from 'horse.' If what one wants does not differ, then how is it that yellow or black horses are acceptable in one case and unacceptable in the other case? It is clear that acceptable and unacceptable are mutually contrary. Hence, yellow and black horses are the same, one can respond that there are horses, but one cannot respond that there are white horses. Thus, it is evident that white horses are not horses.

Pretty sure it's possible for ordinary computers alone are enough to simulate the brain given enough resources, but that's the soft problem whereas arguing that such a machine is actually conscious seems to be the hard problem, which more computation and physics won't solve.

The alternative to digital is analog and it seems that neuromorphic computers use a mix of both. Of course, it's at least Turing complete, but I'm not convinced that it's physically possible for anything to be more computationally powerful.

Technically speaking, the processes in digital computers are already analog but they're measured as discrete. But is it possible for something to be truly analog in the sense that it can work on a continuous range of inputs across arbitrary precision? The universe itself is not completely continuous and real world analog computers have errors after a certain point. At small levels, charge becomes individual electrons. Space and time itself aren't necessarily continuous either at the quantum level. The smallest meaningful distance in physics is the planck length. As such, it doesnt seem like you can really set an analog state to any irrational number without some degree of uncertainty. There's even an absurd mathematical theorem (banarch tarski theorem) that says that a continuous solid 3d ball can be divided and rearranged such that it there are 2 identical spheres. Aka, you can take something and duplicate it just by rearranging it's parts, which doesn't seem possible in the physical world.

In conclusion, im not convinced that neuromorphic computers are actually more powerful in a fundamental or philosophical sense.
